feed.title: Lists, Directories & Discovery — Useful Sites
feed.subtitle: A hand-curated, annotated link directory across ten areas, from software and AI to security, economics and architecture. Every entry states what the resource does and where it parts ways with its neighbours.

entry.title: AtlasRepo
entry.summary: A searchable catalogue of roughly 40,000 open-source projects with summaries, categories and quality scores, also exposed to coding agents via MCP. Unlike star-ranked lists its scoring method is published. A free account and paid plans exist.

entry.title: Awesome Maps+Data
entry.summary: A list of real-time map and data-visualisation sites (aviation, space, weather, history, marine, cyber threats). Unlike general link lists, it only gathers interactive map/data experiences.

entry.title: Awesome Obsidian Vaults
entry.summary: Topic-grouped list of ready-made notes vaults and digital gardens for developers and learners, downloadable for offline use in Obsidian, with automated link checking. Unlike plugin lists, it distributes content (notes).

entry.title: Awesome Web Scraping
entry.summary: A web-scraping list of libraries, services and manuals split by language (Python, PHP, Ruby, JS, Go, CLI). Unlike one library's docs, it lays out the whole ecosystem per language.

entry.title: best-of-digital-gardens
entry.summary: A weekly-updated, star-ranked list of about 100 digital gardens (personal wikis and note sites) whose source lives in a git repository. Unlike hand-curated garden lists, its ranking is generated and kept current automatically.

entry.title: Map All Spaces
entry.summary: Combines hackerspaces, fablabs and makerspaces from SpaceAPI, Fablab.io and the Hackerspaces wiki on one map, with a heatmap of open/closed status. Unlike a single network map it merges several sources.

entry.title: Awesome Awesomeness
entry.summary: A list of awesome lists, grouped by topic. Unlike the sindresorhus/awesome index it is flatter and wider, covering more niche lists.

entry.title: BetaList
entry.summary: Early-access listings for startups that have not launched yet. Unlike Product Hunt it shows pre-launch products, so you meet them before the crowd — the catch being that some never launch.

entry.title: Blogroll.org
entry.summary: A human-curated list of independent personal blogs that are updated regularly, with no algorithm. Unlike a reader’s discovery tab it is a plain list: no ranking, no recommendations.

entry.title: Changelog
entry.summary: Podcasts and a news feed about software development and open source. Unlike general tech podcasts it stays with practitioners: maintainers and builders explaining how they work.

entry.title: daily.dev
entry.summary: A personalised developer news aggregator. Unlike a single curated list it learns your topics and pulls many sources into one feed.

entry.title: DEV Community
entry.summary: A free blogging and discussion community for programmers. Unlike Medium it is developer-only, with tags as the main way to navigate; posts range from beginner tutorials to deep dives.

entry.title: Hacker News
entry.summary: Y Combinator’s link-and-discussion board for programming, startups and technology. Unlike Reddit it is one ranked front page with short, expert-heavy comments; Lobsters is the smaller, invitation-only alternative.

entry.title: Hashnode
entry.summary: A blogging platform for developers where you publish on your own domain. Unlike DEV the blog is yours (custom domain) while still appearing in a shared feed.

entry.title: Indie Hackers
entry.summary: A community where founders share the revenue and strategy behind small products and side projects. Unlike general startup media it publishes the unglamorous detail: what a product actually earned and how it found its first users.

entry.title: Indieblog.page
entry.summary: A discovery site that sends you to a random post from a personal blog at the press of a button. Unlike blog lists you do not choose, so you run into voices you would not have looked for.

entry.title: Lobsters
entry.summary: A smaller computing link board, joined by invitation, with tag-based filtering. Unlike Hacker News it is narrower and slower, with stricter moderation and the option to mute topics.

entry.title: Marginalia Search
entry.summary: A small independent search engine favouring text-heavy sites that ask for no cookies or newsletters. Unlike Google it deliberately downranks SEO-inflated pages: fewer and stranger results, but often better for reading.

entry.title: Product Hunt
entry.summary: A daily, community-voted ranking of newly launched products. Unlike review sites such as G2 it is about what launched today — the quickest way to see what is new, though the ranking rewards launch-day effort more than lasting quality.

entry.title: SaaSHub
entry.summary: A software-alternatives directory: name a product and get comparable tools with side-by-side pages. Unlike AlternativeTo it centres on SaaS and startup products.

entry.title: Sidebar
entry.summary: Five design links every weekday, picked by one curator. Unlike feeds that throw everything at you it limits the choice on purpose, so a minute is enough.

entry.title: StackShare
entry.summary: Shows which tools companies and developers build their products with, one stack page per company. Unlike comparison sites it answers “what do real teams run?” rather than “which is best?”; the data is self-reported and can be out of date.

entry.title: Wiby
entry.summary: A search engine for the classic, lightweight web, with a “surprise me” button. Unlike Marginalia its index is built from pages people submitted, so it is smaller and hand-picked.

entry.title: Awesome Developer-First
entry.summary: A list of products that target developers as the user. Unlike general SaaS lists, it picks only developer-targeted products, usually API- and CLI-first.

entry.title: Awesome Engineering Strategy
entry.summary: A resource list for designing and executing engineering strategy. Unlike general management lists, it focuses on setting technical direction — writing strategy, architecture decisions, technology choices.

entry.title: Awesome Engineering Team Management
entry.summary: A resource list for transitioning from software development into management. Unlike general management books, it focuses on topics specific to engineering teams: hiring, one-on-ones, technical debt, team structure.

entry.title: Awesome Indie
entry.summary: A resource list for building independent developer businesses. Unlike startup and VC-oriented resources, it focuses on building a small, profitable business without outside investment.

entry.title: Awesome Markdown
entry.summary: A list of editors, converters and resources for the Markdown markup language. Unlike a single editor, it brings together editors, converters and dialects such as CommonMark and GFM.

entry.title: Awesome Naming
entry.summary: A list of guides on naming things in computer science. Unlike general style guides, it focuses only on naming — variables, functions, APIs.

entry.title: Awesome OKR
entry.summary: A resource list for OKR goal-setting and communication best practices. Unlike general productivity lists, it gathers guides, examples and tools specific to the OKR method.

entry.title: Awesome Read the Docs
entry.summary: A list of example documentation projects to inspire your own. Unlike documentation-tool lists, it shows examples rather than tools: real projects that are well put together.

entry.title: Awesome Regex
entry.summary: A list of tools and resources for regular expressions (regex), the pattern-matching language. Unlike a single tester such as regex101, it brings together tools, libraries, flavour differences and tutorials; maintained by Steven Levithan, author of XRegExp.

entry.title: Awesome Speakers
entry.summary: A list of conference and meetup speakers in the programming community. Unlike conference sites, it gathers speakers with their topics and links in one list — for organisers.

entry.title: Awesome Stacks
entry.summary: A list of tech stacks used for building different kinds of apps.

entry.title: Awesome Standards
entry.summary: A list of the proposals and standards (RFCs and more) that define the internet and software. Unlike searching RFCs one by one, it groups standards by area — web, networking, security, file formats.

entry.title: Awesome Tech Ethics
entry.summary: A list of ethics resources focused on mitigating technology’s potential harms. Unlike general ethics resources, it targets software and data practice: principles, case studies, courses.

entry.title: Awesome Unicode
entry.summary: A resource list for the Unicode standard, its quirks and its tools. Unlike the standard itself, it demonstrates the quirks — invisible characters, homoglyphs, normalisation — with examples.

entry.title: Awesome Wardley Maps
entry.summary: A list for Wardley Maps, which give situational awareness for strategic decisions.

entry.title: GitHub Octoverse
entry.summary: GitHub’s annual report, showing software trends with data. Unlike survey-based reports the data comes from GitHub’s own platform activity — not what people say, but what they do.

entry.title: Stack Overflow Survey
entry.summary: The annual large survey of developers’ tool, language and salary trends. Unlike reports drawn from platform activity, the data comes from asking developers directly — where the “loved” and “dreaded” technologies are measured.
